query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a nanoscale, functionally graded amorphous surface coating, enriched with tailored additives (e.g., Ti and Zr), on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable a dual-mode operation: at room temperature, the coating will provide intrinsic lubricity due to its amorphous structure, while at elevated temperatures (up to 800 °C) it will transform in situ into a dense, self-adaptive oxide glaze. This adaptive interface will maintain a low coefficient of friction and low wear rate over the full temperature range, overcoming the deterioration seen with the bare alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix that exhibits good room-temperature friction performance but suffers from increased friction and wear at high temperatures due to oxidation, phase instability, and surface degradation.
generation.intervention: Develop and deposit a nanoscale, functionally graded amorphous surface coating with tailored additives such as Ti and Zr.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under controlled loads (e.g., moderate to high normal load such as 30 N), sliding speeds (e.g., 1–5 mm/s), and ambient air environment with a temperature range spanning from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The amorphous coating initially imparts low friction by its intrinsic lubricity and then, upon thermal activation, generates a uniform and dense oxide glaze layer that protects the surface and minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the amorphous coating minimizes friction due to its disordered structure and smooth surface. As the temperature rises, controlled tribo-oxidation transforms the coating into a stable oxide glaze enriched with oxides of the tailored additives (e.g., TiO2, ZrO2), which reduces adhesion and provides wear resistance. This adaptive transformation bridges the performance gap observed in the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi, the coated alloy will maintain a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate throughout the complete temperature range, particularly showing a marked improvement at high temperatures (600–800 °C) where the coating transforms to a protective glaze.
generation.baseline: Performance of the uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, which exhibits low friction at room temperature but deteriorates (increased friction and wear) as temperature approaches 800 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under sliding wear conditions with the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under moderate to high loads (around 30 N) and sliding speeds (around 1–5 mm/s) in an ambient air environment.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports the adaptive formation of oxide glaze layers via controlled tribo-oxidation, the exact kinetics of the amorphous-to-glaze transformation, coating adhesion under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses, and long-term stability of the oxide layer over repeated cycles remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set with the nanoscale, functionally graded amorphous Ti/Zr-containing coating deposited on CoCrFeNi and a control set with the bare CoCrFeNi. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled loads (e.g., 30 N) and sliding speeds (e.g., 1–5 mm/s) while progressively ramping the temperature from room temperature to 800 °C. Periodically record friction coefficients, wear rates, and conduct post-test surface analyses (e.g., SEM and EDS) to assess oxide glaze formation.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Surface morphology and oxide composition via SEM/EDS
Adhesion and integrity of the transformed oxide glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (lower friction coefficient and wear rate) over the bare CoCrFeNi across the full temperature range—particularly failing to form a stable, protective oxide glaze at elevated temperatures—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

decision.trend: Early studies focused on tweaking bulk composition and processing routes to form complex microstructures that could partially address the high‐temperature wear problems. For example, oxide dispersion strengthening (with Y2O3 additions in PMC5706259) and alloying with elements such as W (PMC8470387) or Mo (PMC12655553) improved high‐temperature wear resistance by stabilizing microstructures or forming rigid intermetallics. Meanwhile, approaches like plasma spraying and laser cladding yielded engineered coatings that partly adapted at high temperatures but either suffered friction fluctuations or did not deliver consistent low friction across the entire temperature range. Overall, prior work has gradually shifted from simple composition changes to surface/interface and microstructure architecture modifications to gain a measure of high‐temperature stability, yet none have provided a single intervention that manages both low friction and low wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
decision.unsolved: Maintaining a low coefficient of friction and low wear rate continuously across a broad temperature span remains unachieved; previous interventions tend to optimize one temperature regime at the expense of the other. In particular, how to engineer the sliding interface so that it adapts dynamically—from mediating lubricity in the room‐temperature regime to forming a stable, protective oxide layer at high temperatures—remains an open challenge.
decision.lever: Developing and depositing a nanoscale, functionally graded amorphous surface coating (incorporating tailored additives like Ti and Zr) that is designed to transform in situ into a dense, self-adaptive oxide glaze at elevated temperatures
decision.why: This direction follows the observed trend that surface treatments can leverage in situ tribo-chemical reactions to form protective layers at high temperatures (as seen in HEA film studies such as PMC10456374) without altering the inherently useful CoCrFeNi matrix at room temperature. By targeting the sliding interface, the coating can be engineered to offer low friction through intrinsic lubricity at lower temperatures and transition to a robust, anti-wear oxide layer near 800 °C, bridging the performance gap identified in prior studies.
